 --> Naraka Chaturdashi 2026: Date, Abhyanga Snan and Puja Timings
 Naraka Chaturdashi 2026 falls on November 8. Check the Choti Diwali date, Abhyanga Snan muhurat, Chaturdashi Tithi timings, rituals and religious significance.

 Naraka Chaturdashi 2026: Date, Abhyanga Snan and Puja Timings (image: canva) Naraka Chaturdashi 2026 is on Sunday, November 8.
 Abhyanga Snan muhurat is from 5:41 am to 6:38 am.
 The festival symbolises the triumph of good over evil.

 Naraka Chaturdashi 2026 will be observed on Sunday, November 8, in India. Also known as Choti Diwali, Roop Chaturdashi and Roop Chaudas, the festival is marked by the traditional Abhyanga Snan, a sacred pre-dawn bath believed to purify the body and ward off negative energies. Devotees observing the festival can check the Naraka Chaturdashi date, Abhyanga Snan muhurat, Chaturdashi Tithi timings and associated rituals. 
 According to Drik Panchang, the Abhyanga Snan muhurat in New Delhi will be from 5:41 am to 6:38 am on November 8. The 57-minute window is calculated for the ritual to be performed during moonrise, before sunrise, while Chaturdashi Tithi is prevailing. 
 Naraka Chaturdashi holds an important place in the five-day Diwali celebrations. The day is associated with the victory of good over evil and is observed through traditional bathing rituals, prayers and the lighting of lamps. 
 Naraka Chaturdashi 2026 Date and Abhyanga Snan Muhurat 
 Naraka Chaturdashi falls on the 14th day of the Krishna Paksha in the Hindu lunar month of Kartik. The festival is widely celebrated as Choti Diwali and is considered one of the most significant days of the Diwali period.  Here are the key details for Naraka Chaturdashi 2026: 
 Naraka Chaturdashi date: Sunday, November 8, 2026 
 Abhyanga Snan muhurat: 5:41 am to 6:38 am 
 Duration: 57 minutes 
 Moonrise at Abhyanga Snan: 5:41 am 
 Chaturdashi Tithi begins: 10:47 am on November 7, 2026 
 Chaturdashi Tithi ends: 11:27 am on November 8, 2026 
 The timings are based on the New Delhi Panchang. Since sunrise and moonrise vary across locations, devotees in other cities should consult their local Panchang for the exact Abhyanga Snan muhurat. Chaturdashi Tithi Timings for Naraka Chaturdashi 2026 
 The Chaturdashi Tithi will begin at 10:47 am on November 7 and end at 11:27 am on November 8.  The Abhyanga Snan ritual is performed during the pre-dawn period, when Chaturdashi Tithi is in effect. The timing is significant because Hindu religious traditions prescribe the bath during the period between moonrise and sunrise. 
 In 2026, Naraka Chaturdashi falls on November 8. The date is determined by the prevailing Tithi and the prescribed ritual window, rather than simply by the Gregorian calendar. 
 What is Abhyanga Snan? Rituals and significance 
 Abhyanga Snan is a traditional oil bath performed during the Diwali festivities. On Naraka Chaturdashi, devotees commonly apply sesame oil, known as til oil, to the body before taking a bath. The ritual is often accompanied by the use of ubtan, a traditional herbal cleansing paste.  The bath is considered a symbolic act of purification and renewal. According to Hindu belief, performing Abhyanga Snan on Naraka Chaturdashi is believed to help devotees avoid Narak, or hell, and cleanse themselves of negative influences. 
 The ritual is regarded as especially significant on Chaturdashi. While Abhyanga Snan is also prescribed on Amavasya and Pratipada during the Diwali period, the observance on Naraka Chaturdashi is considered the most important. 
 Why is Naraka Chaturdashi also called Choti Diwali? 
 Naraka Chaturdashi is popularly known as Choti Diwali, Roop Chaturdashi and Roop Chaudas. The festival is associated with the legend of Lord Krishna’s defeat of the demon Narakasura.  According to Hindu mythology, Narakasura had caused widespread suffering. His defeat by Lord Krishna symbolised the triumph of righteousness over evil. The occasion is therefore observed with prayers, ritual bathing and the lighting of lamps. 
 In many parts of India, Choti Diwali is marked by decorating homes with diyas, preparing sweets and making arrangements for the main Diwali celebrations. Customs may differ according to regional traditions and family practices. 
 Naraka Chaturdashi and Kali Chaudas: Are they the same? 
 Naraka Chaturdashi and Kali Chaudas are often considered the same festival, but they are distinct religious observances associated with the Chaturdashi Tithi.  Naraka Chaturdashi is linked to the defeat of Narakasura and the tradition of Abhyanga Snan. Kali Chaudas, observed particularly in parts of western India, is associated with the worship of Goddess Kali and regional religious customs. 
 Depending on the beginning and ending of Chaturdashi Tithi, the two observances may fall on the same date or on two consecutive days. Devotees are advised to follow their local Panchang for the appropriate observance. 
 Diwali 2026: Five-day festival and important dates 
 The traditional Diwali festivities begin with Dhanteras and conclude with Bhai Dooj. Each day carries its own religious and cultural significance. 
 Dhanteras: November 6, 2026 
 Naraka Chaturdashi or Choti Diwali: November 8, 2026 
 Diwali or Lakshmi Puja: November 8, 2026 
 Govardhan Puja: November 9, 2026 
 Bhai Dooj: November 11, 2026 
 In 2026, Naraka Chaturdashi and the main Diwali Lakshmi Puja fall on the same day. Devotees will observe Abhyanga Snan during the early morning hours and perform Lakshmi Puja in the evening. 
 How to observe Naraka Chaturdashi 2026 
 Devotees can begin the day with Abhyanga Snan during the prescribed muhurat. Sesame oil is traditionally used for the ritual, followed by a bath before sunrise.  After the bath, families may offer prayers, light diyas and prepare their homes for the Diwali celebrations. In several regions, the day also includes traditional offerings and rituals connected with the Narakasura legend. 
 Naraka Chaturdashi is a day of spiritual significance, symbolising the cleansing of negativity and the victory of good over evil. With the correct Abhyanga Snan muhurat and Tithi timings, devotees can observe the festival in accordance with their religious traditions.
